_about: The half of doc/ROADMAP.md that a person has to write down, because
nothing in the repository knows it.
`omacar roadmap` derives everything countable -- lines, tests, profiles,
coverage, what git shipped -- and never reads it from here. This file
holds only the three things a checkout genuinely cannot answer:
inflight  what is being built right now, each naming the file that will
exist once it lands. The generator asks git whether that file
is tracked and marks the item landed or not. Nobody has to
remember to move a line, which is the usual way an in-flight
list ends up describing work that shipped a month ago.
`branch` names where the work is happening. Remove an item once
it has landed; doc/capabilities.json records what shipped.
claims    assertions made in the prose that nothing here can check --
a price comparison, a piece of arithmetic, a negative result.
Each carries the date it was last checked and a human-readable
`how`. The generator NEVER executes `how`. A JSON file in a
public repository that a maintenance command shells out to is
a remote code execution waiting for whoever pulls a branch.
A claim that came from outside carries `sources`, the https
addresses it came from, and `verified`: true when the number
was seen on that page, false when it was not. `omacar roadmap
--check` refuses a claim missing its date or its `how`, and a
sourced claim that does not say whether it was verified.
field     the car and the world: drives, demos, the things that happened
away from the keyboard. Append a dated line; do not rewrite
old ones. A journal is the one hand-maintained document that
does not rot -- when somebody stops keeping it, it stops, it
does not start lying.

inflight.title: The foundation redesign: Vehicle, the looks, and review screenshots
inflight.note: The frame, Home, private assets and the layout editor have landed. Left: Vehicle (task 8), the advisor on Opus 5.5 (task 9, inside lib/ai.py) and the looks (task 10, inside existing files), then the screenshot tool that sets the screens beside the mockups. See doc/design/2026-09-28-foundation-plan.md.

inflight.title: Cameras and drowsy mode, for the 2026-09-30 drive
inflight.note: Three wired cameras recorded on the tablet, hard-braking locks, the Cameras tab from mockup 6, and a drowsy mode that watches the driver's eyes and escalates through three ramped alerts, always 12 dB over the music. Designed in doc/design/2026-09-28-cameras-drowsy.md on that branch.

inflight.title: Drive-day hardening: the recorder outlives a vanishing adapter
inflight.note: Lands inside lib/drivelog.py, lib/preflight.py, share/systemd/omacar-drivelog.service, doc/drive-day.md and test/guards_test.py, all of which exist, so git cannot tell you whether it is done. Confirm with `git log --oneline -- lib/drivelog.py` showing 'The recorder loses a leg to a vanishing adapter now, not the whole day'.

claims.text: Snap-on's flagship ZEUS+ (EEMS348) lists at $11,792 and its entry MT2600 at $1,895, US MSRP. Keeping a ZEUS current costs $1,235 a year on subscription.
claims.how: Open the two product pages, and the newest pocket guide for the subscription. The 25.4 guide (dated 2025-09-29) was still the newest published on 2026-09-28; look for a 26.x one first. Nobody pays MSRP on hardware, so this is the ceiling, not the typical price.

claims.text: Autel's own store sells the MaxiSYS Ultra S2 at $6,499 and the MS906 Pro at $1,569 (regularly $1,599). Launch's X431 PAD VII Elite is $2,499 from the Launch store on Amazon. A reseller lists a year of Ultra updates at $899.
claims.how: Open each page. Autel's own store sells no update renewal, so the $899 is a reseller's figure; treat it as indicative. Store prices move with sales.

claims.text: A shop charges $125 to $183 in labour to diagnose a check engine light (RepairPal's national range, page dated 2026-09-03), and O'Reilly says a shop charges around $100 just to read the codes. AutoZone and O'Reilly read codes for free.
claims.how: Open the RepairPal estimator and the two parts-store pages. RepairPal's range excludes taxes, fees and location; a free parts-store read gives the code, not the diagnosis, which is the gap this project fills.

claims.text: OBDLink's MX+ costs $139.95 and its EX $69.95 from OBDLink; the wired SX this project was developed on is $49.95 and was out of stock. A basic handheld code reader (ANCEL AD310) is $23.99.
claims.how: Open the pages. These are the adapter prices the hardware guide quotes.

claims.text: Generic ELM327 Bluetooth clones sell for roughly $6 to $17.
claims.how: Seen in an Amazon search on 2026-09-28 by the research pass, including sponsored listings; a search page is not a stable citation and could not be re-fetched. Search a marketplace for 'ELM327 Bluetooth' and read the first page.

claims.text: Cheap ELM327 clones typically copy the old v1.4 firmware, bugs included, and report a version they are not, such as v1.5 or v2.1.
claims.how: The Wikipedia article's section on clones. A better source is a first-hand test: `omacar doctor` against a clone, recording what it claims and what it does.

claims.text: rtl_433 has no decoder for Tymate tyre sensors: the name appears nowhere in its device list, sources or configs as of commit 02cd4b6 (2026-09-26).
claims.how: Search the repository for 'Tymate'. Then settle it properly, as decided on 2026-09-28: once the RTL-SDR arrives, record the owner's TM2 sensors at 433.92 MHz for about an hour with rtl_433's generic and flex decoders. A recording that decodes makes this claim irrelevant; buying sensors rtl_433 already supports is the fallback only if it does not.

claims.text: The RTL-SDR Blog V4 reached end of line in May 2026; its replacement, the V4L, is $37.95. The u-blox NEO-M9V does both untethered and automotive dead reckoning, and a module with a pin header sells for about EUR 70.
claims.how: Open the pages. The rtl-sdr.com blog also warns of fake V4s on marketplaces, which the hardware guide should repeat.

claims.text: OBDb, the community signal-set project lib/knowledge.py reads, had 746 public repositories on 2026-09-28, under CC BY-SA 4.0.
claims.how: The organisation page, or the GitHub API's public_repos count for the OBDb org.

claims.text: Piper's active repository, OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl, is GPL-3.0; the MIT-licensed rhasspy/piper is archived and says development has moved. OmaCar therefore does not bundle Piper: it is installed as a system package and run as its own program, and the voice clips it renders are ordinary audio files.
claims.how: Open both repositories and read their licence files. If the licence of the maintained version changes, the reason for not bundling it goes away; the decision of 2026-09-28 still stands until the owner revisits it.

claims.text: The Omarchy manual points plugin authors to omarchyplugins.com as the community plugin directory, run from a repository in the same organisation as Omarchy; its registry listed about 4,400 entries on 2026-09-28.
claims.how: Open the manual page and the marketplace repository, and count the entries in its registry.json. The compatibility analysis in the capability map starts here and at /usr/share/omarchy/shell/plugins on an Omarchy machine.

claims.text: A full sweep of the manufacturer identifier range is about seventy minutes per module.
claims.how: Arithmetic: the identifier count above, at the pacing lib/autodisc.py actually uses. Time one real burst with `omacar discover` and divide.

claims.text: Pre-CAN protocol support (J1850, ISO 9141-2, KWP2000) is written from the ELM327 datasheet and the ISO documents and has never been run against a pre-CAN car.
claims.how: Run `omacar doctor` on a pre-1996-protocol vehicle. The moment somebody does, this claim and roadmap item 2.5 both change, and every protocol entry that says 'untested' has to be re-read.

claims.text: Service 0x21 -- the pre-UDS live-data service, and the most likely remaining home for live IMA values -- has never been asked of the CR-Z's hybrid controllers with a correctly shaped 29-bit header.
claims.how: The only 0x21 sweep on record used header 07E0, an 11-bit address, on a car running CAN 29/500; it is uninformative rather than a negative result. Two minutes parked with the engine running settles it: `omacar prospect --service 0x21 --headers 18DA03F1,18DA04F1,18DA10F1,18DA0EF1 --range 00-FF --parked`.

claims.text: Generic mode 01 PID 0x5B, hybrid battery remaining life, appears in this car's own supported-PID bitmap and has never once been polled.
claims.how: One request. A support bitmap is a claim the ECU makes about itself, not a reading, and bitmaps overstate. Ask it before anything is built on it.

claims.text: The IMA repair-frequency shares, part number and cell-block figures in share/data/dtc.json are unsourced, and the code they document (P1449) is not in this car's own fault catalogue.
claims.how: The file's own _about says the shares come from published repair-frequency data but names no source, and its Mode 06 citations match the simulator rather than the car. Either cite a source that was actually read, or mark the entry unsourced. Until then it must not be surfaced as relevant to the CR-Z.

field.what: First real-car session on the CR-Z. Protocol identified as ISO 15765-4 (CAN 29/500), the two hybrid controllers found awake on 29-bit headers, and -- after service 0x22 came back empty across thousands of identifiers -- the service 0x19 fault catalogues found, which is where the Honda-specific data actually was.

Three legs in one day: Marina to Los Banos to San Francisco and home, logging the whole way. The longest continuous real-world run the tool has had, and the first time it was judged on whether it was pleasant to sit next to for hours rather than on whether it read a PID.

Demonstrated at the Silicon Valley / San Francisco Omarchy meetup at Cloudflare HQ. The feedback was that it was the strongest project shown and that the UI and UX need a higher level of polish. Both halves of that are recorded on this page: the first is the field validation the roadmap had been missing, and the second is now a named gap rather than a compliment nobody wrote down.
